In light of the fact that EC position, being the German position, actually, was contravening the doctrine of international law, as well as the position of the UN, one learned scholar, Lori Fisher Damrosch, said, I'll quote: "Neither the multilateralisation of Germany's initiative within the framework of the EC, nor the fact that the EC acted after following what was purported to be a judicial proceeding, should suffice to resolve doubts about the legitimacy about premature recognition, at least not against the urgent plea of the Secretary-General for all states to refrain from selective recognition outside the framework of an overall political settlement. The Security Council had explicitly approved the Secretary-General's report, which embodied the plea to refrain from premature recognition. The EC's disregard of his appeal should therefore be considered legally suspect."

Three constitutive nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina under communist regime succeeded to maintain mutual tolerance and internal stability. The same solution is enshrined in the present constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is an integral part of the Dayton peace accord. The critical moment in Bosnia occurred in October 1991, when the Serb deputies in the republic parliament were outvoted by Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. The Bosnian Serbs had no choice but to protect their own vital interests by way of a referendum and the establishment of their own entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina. We heard from the Prosecutor side that they want to rely on a document issued by Crisis Staff, renaming the name of Bosanski Samac into Samac, and they want to make this relation with the common intent or particular individual intent of persecution, which means that for the non-Serb population, this moment is very scareful [sic]. They are getting to be nervous and they want to leave this region. Remember that document. I would like now to present the fact that the name Samac dates back to 17th century. It is not 1992. It is 17th century. The etymology of the word "Samac" is this: It comes from the German word schanze, s-c-h-a-n-z-e, meaning a military trench. At that time the town was in fact a military settlement during the Austro-Turkish war, and wishing to maintain the local tradition of the town, during 1992 local authorities renamed Bosanski Samac into Samac because Bosanski Samac was the origin imputed by the Austro-Hungarian empire at the beginning of the 13th century. It was not original. Inevitably, Bosanski Samac was, you know, by force named. And then Samac is more -- on the other hand, Samac is more general, and also based on the historical fact. So this is really something which I must outline, because it is not usual in opening statement to make these relations. But when we come to this exhibit during the course of trial, I will provide this Trial Chamber with further facts and information. Now we are seeing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We've gone beyond the ten minutes, Mr. Pantelic. One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have only legal issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the interpreters are overworked, so are you winding up in five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, five minutes. I'm absolutely fine, yes. The Prosecution is trying to persuade this Court that the process of ethnic cleansing was carried out on the territory of Samac municipality, whereby, inter alia, Dr. Blagoje Simic allegedly committed the war crime, a crime of persecution as charged under count 1 of the indictment. The Defence shall prove that none of the elements of this offence can be found in the acts of Dr. Blagoje Simic. Assuming that even if crimes of persecution were committed, they could only be ascribed to paramilitary and police forces with which Dr. Simic had no relevant connections that could point to his possible criminal responsibility. Apart from that, there is no nexus between Dr. Simic's acts and consequences that could be qualified as persecution. The essence of this complex legal issue in brief form is as follows: Where there are, within the temporal and territorial scope of the indictment, such acts committed on the territory of Samac municipality could be qualified as persecution. The Defence will show that they cannot be qualified as persecution. Assuming that such actions did take place, were they widespread and systematic or were they in fact isolated events of low intensity and in the form of separate incident? Even if there were such actions committed by other perpetrators, the question is whether they stood in any sort of causal relationship with Dr. Simic; and if so, what was the form of scope and that relationship? With regard to this issue, I would like to outline the possibility that elements of persecution on political, racial, and religious grounds, which is Article 5(h), did exist in the acts of the members of police and paramilitary units; yes, indeed. But I categorically deny any possibility that Dr. Simic, who acted in capacity of Crisis Staff president, can be found guilty for crimes against humanity under Article 5(h) of the Statute solely based on his activities. What sort of persecution are we talking about if throughout the existence of the armed conflict, members of the non-Serb exercised important functions within municipal authorities, public institutions, hospital? What sort of persecution is it when in conditions of war municipal authorities organised life in the best possible way under those circumstances for all the inhabitants of Samac, regardless of their ethnic origin? And what sort of persecution are we talking about if all inhabitants, regardless of their nationality and despite significant difficulties caused by the war, are being provided with the best possible health care? What sort of persecution is it if everyone, regardless of nationality, is being paid salaries, and even receive financial compensation for legitimate compulsory wartime working obligation? With regard to the Prosecution position concerning count 2, crimes against humanity; deportation, under Article 5(d); and count 3, grave breaches of Geneva Conventions of 1949; unlawful deportation or transfer or unlawful confinement of a civilian under Article 2(g) of the indictment, the Defence emphasises that pursuant to the latest jurisprudence of this Tribunal and the doctrine of continental criminal law, cumulative charges are not permissible, and we shall rely on this document during the course of trial. Actually --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone is off, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe you should continue tomorrow, because we are really running over the time for the interpreters. We'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me one minute, I will finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: One minute, okay. Just one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, Dr. Simic has no relation whatsoever with the events which took place in Odzak municipality. In that particular town, a military administration was established, which basically meant that the civil administration had no power over it. Even Prosecution provided the evidence to that effect, so I cannot see any viable reason to charge Mr. Simic on these grounds. Your Honours, in brief words, who is Dr. Blagoje Simic? You have in front of you a man dedicated to humanity, a doctor of medicine by education, a family man, a father of three children, and an exemplary husband. In his life, Dr. Simic only helped people. He was bound to do this not only because of the Hippocratic oath but also because of the family system and the ethics, the value system which in his education he received from his parents. The Defence will prove that this man is not criminally responsible for the alleged crimes charged against him. Finally, Your Honours, in this court of law, you are here to try solely by the law and book and on the basis of fact. This Tribunal does not try political beliefs, despite the Prosecution endeavours to present this case as a part of broader policy of Bosnian Serbs being members of criminal enterprise at top levels, et cetera, et cetera. I believe in this Court, Your Honours, and Dr. Blagoje Simic too, he believes in this Court. He voluntarily surrendered and put himself under the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. He is absolutely convinced of his innocence, and he is convinced that he will free himself of the unjust allegation the Prosecution charges him with. By presenting his defence, he would not be only defending himself, but also his family, his town, his neighbours, Republika Srpska, and all Serb people. For Dr. Blagoje Simic, I think, by the outcome of these proceedings, the only possible decision will be not guilty. Thank you very much, Madam President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Two quick announcements. Mr. Pantelic, the video footage had no transcript. There were scenes where people were discussing, especially where they were discussing stopping motorists, which can easily be interpreted by our interpreters of the Tribunal, and can we have that transcript prepared, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, yes. I have an internal version - it's a part of my evidence - of one hour and a half. So I will prepare in each part of this genuine videotape all transcripts treated to all these events, and in due course I will provide it to my colleagues and also one copy to the Trial Chamber, you can be sure. Because this one is just a selected one, and I don't want to make -- to have an impression that it's kind of manipulation of the acts. So it was just based on the principle of judicial economy, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like to ask the Prosecution to number the paragraphs in the statement of Mr. Donia, the first witness tomorrow. If we can have the paragraphs numbered, it is much easier to refer to a specific paragraph should the issue arise. So I would be grateful if that can be done before tomorrow. The proceedings will adjourn. At 1500 hours we will sit for a Status Conference involving counsel only. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours pleases, might I just raise one very brief matter? That's this afternoon. If possible, and if it would help the Chamber, would it be a sensible idea for myself and also for Defence counsel to approach the legal officers of the Tribunal at about 2.30 to get an idea of the sort of issues that the Chamber is interested in, the sorts of things that they want to hear answers to this afternoon, so that we can be prepared and come here with answers rather than having to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is a good idea, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I suggest that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give instructions to the legal officer. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
